opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to the way machine learning as a field actually makes progress. If you look at the history of AI over the last decade or so, a huge amount of the progress has been organized around benchmarks and environments. ImageNet is the classic example, but you see it with Atari, with Go, with StarCraft, with the various language benchmarks. Researchers are drawn to well-defined problems where they can measure progress, compare against each other, and publish. A good benchmark acts like a coordination point for the whole community: it tells thousands of very talented people, "Here's a problem worth working on, and here's how you'll know if you've made headway."

So if you care about cooperative capabilities, the skills that let AI systems, and humans with AI systems, find mutually beneficial outcomes, communicate credibly, make and keep commitments, and avoid destructive conflict, then one of the most efficient things you can do is build the environments where those skills get exercised and measured. Historically, a lot of multi-agent research has been framed around zero-sum games. Chess, Go, poker, and StarCraft are all fundamentally about beating an opponent. That's produced remarkable systems, but it means the field has been optimizing for competitive intelligence much more than cooperative intelligence. Most of the important problems in the real world aren't zero-sum, though. They're mixed-motive: there are gains from cooperation, but also temptations to defect, problems of trust, and problems of bargaining over how to divide the surplus.

The leverage comes from the fact that building a really good environment is a relatively small investment compared to the amount of research effort it can redirect. If you design something like Diplomacy, or Melting Pot-style social dilemma suites, or negotiation tasks, and they catch on, you've shifted the attention of a large research community toward questions that matter for safety and for good societal outcomes. You've also created shared vocabulary and evaluation tools, so when someone claims their agent is more cooperative, there's a way to check that.

There's a second reason, which is about evaluation as AI systems get deployed. We're moving into a world where AI agents will increasingly interact with each other on behalf of people, firms, and maybe governments: negotiating, transacting, and coordinating. We'd really like to know in advance whether those agents tend toward collusion against third parties, whether they escalate conflicts, whether they can be exploited, and whether they can reach fair agreements. You can't answer those questions without environments that probe them. So benchmarks aren't just a way to spur capability development; they're the infrastructure for understanding how these systems behave in social settings before the stakes get high.

And I'd add one caveat, which is that you have to be thoughtful about it. Cooperation isn't always good. Cooperation among a subset of agents can be collusion that harms everyone else. So a well-designed cooperative AI benchmark should reward the kinds of cooperation that are broadly beneficial, and that's a subtle design problem in itself. But that subtlety is part of why I think it's worth people's careful attention: getting the targets right early shapes a lot of what follows.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks let researchers measure progress and compare, but does not propose that research groups compete on benchmark-measured cooperative skill.

r002.rationale: It explains that a benchmark gives researchers a defined problem and a way to know whether they have made progress, motivating work toward a concrete target.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it is that the machine learning community has this enormous capacity to make progress on whatever it's been pointed at, and what points it is largely benchmarks and environments. ImageNet is the classic example: once you had a shared dataset and a leaderboard, you got this explosion of progress on image recognition, because thousands of researchers could compete and compare and build on each other. The same thing happened with Atari and then with things like Go and StarCraft for reinforcement learning. The field is, in a sense, a kind of optimisation process, and the benchmark is the objective function.

And when you look at what the existing benchmarks reward, it's overwhelmingly either single-agent competence, or in the multi-agent setting, zero-sum competition: beating the opponent. That's not an accident; those problems are clean and easy to score. But it means we're pouring a huge amount of talent and compute into making AI systems that are good at winning, and comparatively little into making them good at the thing that actually matters most for humans, which is the mixed-motive situation: where there's some overlap of interests and some conflict, and the question is whether you can find the deal, build trust, communicate credibly, resist the temptation to defect. Most of human life is like that, and most of the situations where AI systems will be deployed together, and alongside humans, will be like that too.

So the leverage comes from the fact that you don't have to do all the research yourself. If you can construct a good environment, where cooperative capabilities, things like understanding other agents, communicating, making commitments, forming institutions, are what actually gets you a high score, then you've recruited the whole field. You've changed what "progress" means for a lot of people, and they'll generate ideas you'd never have thought of.

There's a second reason, which is more defensive. Capabilities are going to improve regardless. The worry is that we get systems that are extremely capable in the strategic, competitive sense but have very undeveloped cooperative intelligence, and then we put them in a world full of other agents. That's a recipe for bad equilibria: arms races, collusion failures, costly bargaining breakdown, the kinds of things humans do to each other but faster and at scale. So I want cooperative capabilities to be developed at least in step with the rest, and benchmarks are the main tool we have for shifting the allocation of effort.

I'd add the caveat that it's genuinely hard to do well. It's easy to build an environment that's gameable, where the "cooperative" behaviour is really just a trick that doesn't generalise, or where you end up rewarding something like collusion against a third party, which isn't what we want either. So part of the research programme is figuring out what the right problems are, not just publishing a leaderboard. But if we get that right, I think it's one of the few things where a relatively small group of people can bend the trajectory of a very large field.

r001.rationale: The response describes a benchmark where cooperative capabilities earn a high score and says it would recruit the field, drawing on the example of researchers competing and comparing through a leaderboard.

r002.rationale: It explains that benchmarks define the objective and that a cooperative benchmark would redirect research effort by making cooperative capabilities a concrete target for high scores.

astra-6.text:
One reason is that a good environment can make an otherwise quite abstract research problem concrete. We can say that we want AI systems to cooperate, but what does that mean in practice? Where does cooperation break down? Is it because the systems don’t understand each other, because they can’t make credible commitments, or because they have conflicting interests? An environment lets us isolate some of those difficulties and study whether we’re actually making progress.

And benchmarks can have a large effect on where research effort goes. If you give researchers an interesting, tractable challenge, with a way to measure improvement, you can get a whole community working on it. So the leverage isn’t just that you personally learn something from building the environment. It’s that you potentially enable many other people to work on the problem.

The tricky part is making sure that success in the benchmark captures something we care about. You wouldn’t want to reward an agent merely for doing well against a fixed set of partners, if what you really want is an ability to cooperate with unfamiliar systems or with humans. And you wouldn’t want to equate cooperation with helping your immediate partner at everyone else’s expense.

So I think there’s substantial intellectual work in designing these environments: identifying the important obstacles to cooperation, representing them in a form we can experiment with, and making the resulting challenges accessible to the broader machine learning community.

r001.rationale: It discusses benchmarks and research communities, but does not propose having research groups compete on their agents’ cooperative skill.

r002.rationale: It says an interesting, tractable challenge with a way to measure improvement can motivate researchers and draw a community to the problem.

sol-6.1.text:
A lot of progress in AI is driven by having a clear task and a way of measuring how well you’re doing. If you have a benchmark where improvements are legible, researchers can try different approaches, compare results, and build on one another’s work. So one way to encourage progress on cooperation is to create environments in which cooperation is both important and measurable.

The challenge is that we don’t just want agents that get a high score when paired with copies of themselves. We want agents that can cooperate with unfamiliar partners, with different capabilities and different preferences. Can they communicate what they want? Can they find opportunities for mutual benefit? Can they make credible commitments, or avoid a conflict that leaves everyone worse off?

And you have to be careful about what you reward. An agent that always gives in might look cooperative by one measure, but it could be very easy to exploit. Similarly, two agents might cooperate very effectively with each other while imposing costs on everyone else. So designing these environments forces us to clarify what kinds of cooperation we actually want.

If we get that right, the benefit isn’t just one research result. It’s infrastructure that allows a whole community to work on these problems, and makes cooperative capabilities a more explicit target of AI development.

r001.rationale: It describes researchers comparing results and building on one another’s work, but does not propose research groups competing on benchmark-measured cooperative skill.

r002.rationale: It explains that a benchmark makes progress on cooperation measurable and gives researchers a clear target to improve.
